titleText.es: Por otro lado, a los físicos les gusta decir que la física es a la matemática lo que el sexo a la masturbación.
titleText.en: On the other hand, physicists like to say physics is to math as sex is to masturbation.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive preserves the same separate analogy as the official English title text.

applications.explanationEn: Campos supplies the ranked items, ordenados describes their arrangement, and por introduces pureza as the criterion used for that ranking.

excludedUnits.rationale: The arrow shows the direction of increasing purity and is not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: LA SOCIOLOGÍA NO ES MÁS QUE PSICOLOGÍA APLICADA.

applications.exampleEs: NO ES MÁS QUE PSICOLOGÍA APLICADA
applications.explanationEn: No and es establish the negative identity frame, más que restricts what remains, and psicología aplicada fills the resulting description.
The field name psicología comes first and aplicada follows it as the neutral descriptive order.
Aplicada uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun psicología.

applications.exampleEs: ESTÁ BIEN ESTAR EN LA CIMA
applications.explanationEn: Está bien supplies the evaluation, while estar remains in its unchanged dictionary form and en la cima completes the location being evaluated.

regions.labelEs: AH, HOLA. NO OS HABÍA VISTO DESDE TAN LEJOS.

applications.explanationEn: Os marks the several people addressed informally, a plural form especially common in Spain.
Había is the past helper and visto is ver's completed-action form, placing the seeing before the moment of speaking.
Tan goes immediately before lejos to intensify the distance as “so far.”

regions.labelEs: SOCIÓLOGOS PSICÓLOGOS BIÓLOGOS QUÍMICOS FÍSICOS MATEMÁTICOS

cards.noteEn: Campo can mean a physical field, but in an academic context it means an area of knowledge or study. Campos is its plural.

example.es: La historia y la química son campos distintos.
example.en: History and chemistry are different fields.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what criterion is used to order or rank a set of things?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ordenar, then por before the criterion used for the order.
cards.noteEn: The things can come first when ordenado functions as a description: libros ordenados por autor. Ordenado changes to match them: ordenada, ordenados, or ordenadas.

example.es: La lista está ordenada por fecha.
example.en: The list is ordered by date.

cards.promptEs: campos ordenados por pureza · ciencias aplicadas · matemáticas
cards.answerEn: the comic ranks academic fields by how abstract or theoretical they appear
cards.noteEn: Each field dismisses the one to its left as merely an applied form of itself. Mathematics is drawn farthest from practical application, which makes the distance itself part of the joke.
Ordenados describes several masculine or mixed items placed in an order. In a heading, that order can be a ranking by some criterion.

example.es: Los resultados están ordenados por fecha.
example.en: The results are ordered by date.

cards.noteEn: Por can identify the feature used to sort or organize things. In a heading, por causa means that the entries are grouped according to their cause.

example.en: We sort the books by topic.

cards.noteEn: Pureza is the quality of being pure. It can be literal, or figurative when an idea is presented as abstract and free from practical complications.

example.es: El laboratorio mide la pureza del agua.
example.en: The laboratory measures the purity of the water.

cards.noteEn: Puros is the masculine plural form of puro. In a ranking of academic fields, it describes fields as more abstract or theoretical rather than more practical.

example.en: They are looking for pure materials.

cards.noteEn: Sociología is the study of societies, social relationships, and institutions.

example.en: She studies sociology at the university.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is nothing but, or only, a particular thing?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a form of ser, then más que and the thing or description that remains.
cards.noteEn: Ser means “to be” and changes for time and subject: no es más que, no era más que, no fue más que. Más que normally introduces a comparison, but inside this negative frame it restricts the subject to only what follows.

example.es: La llamada no fue más que una broma.
example.en: The call was nothing but a joke.

cards.answerEn: no more than; only (as part of no ser más que)
cards.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” Between a negative form of ser and que, it helps restrict something to the description that follows.

example.es: No fue más que un error.
example.en: It was nothing more than a mistake.

cards.answerEn: than; no separate word in the full expression “nothing but”
cards.noteEn: In no ser más que, que completes the restriction introduced by más. The form of ser changes for the person and time.

example.es: Eso no es más que una idea.
example.en: That is nothing but an idea.

cards.noteEn: Psicología is the study of the mind, behavior, and mental processes.

example.es: La psicología estudia la conducta humana.
example.en: Psychology studies human behavior.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: applied; put to practical use (feminine singular)
cards.noteEn: In the name or description of a field, aplicada contrasts practical use with more abstract theory. Use feminine singular aplicada with a feminine singular field name, such as física or lingüística.

example.es: El curso trata de lingüística aplicada.
example.en: The course is about applied linguistics.

cards.noteEn: Biología is the scientific study of living things.

example.es: La biología estudia los seres vivos.
example.en: Biology studies living things.

cards.noteEn: Química is the science of substances, their properties, and how they change.

example.en: We have a chemistry class.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: In está bien followed by an action, está introduces a general judgment. Spanish does not add a separate word for English “it.”

example.en: It is good to ask for help.

cards.promptEs: estar bien + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action or state is good, nice, fine, or acceptable?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of estar followed by bien, then put the verb that names the action or state in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by.” The form of estar can change with time or uncertainty: está bien, estaría bien, or puede que estuviera bien. Spanish does not need a separate subject meaning “it” in this general evaluation. The following verb remains in the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir: preguntar, ser, or salir.

example.en: It is fine to change your mind.

cards.answerEn: to be (in a state or condition)
cards.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used for states, conditions, and locations. After another conjugated verb, estar itself remains unchanged.

example.en: I want to be calm.

cards.noteEn: Cima is the highest point of a mountain or, figuratively, the top position in a ranking.

example.es: Llegaron a la cima de la montaña.
example.en: They reached the summit of the mountain.

cards.noteEn: Ah can show that the speaker has just understood, noticed, or recognized something. Its exact English equivalent depends on tone.

example.en: Oh, yes, now I remember.

cards.answerEn: to you all; you all (informal plural, used mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Os is the short object form used with vosotros or vosotras. It identifies several informally addressed people as receiving or being affected by an action.

example.en: I am sending you all a photo.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.answerEn: had (helper for an earlier completed action)
cards.noteEn: Before a completed-action form such as escrito, había is a past form of the helper haber. It places one completed action before another point in the past.

example.en: I had already eaten when you called.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something had already happened before another past moment?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching past form of haber, then the action verb's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: Use había for I, he, she, or one thing; habías for informal singular “you”; habíamos for “we”; habíais for informal plural “you” in Spain; and habían for “they” or plural formal “you.” The second verb uses a completed-action form, called a past participle: most -ar verbs end in -ado and most -er or -ir verbs end in -ido, although some are irregular, such as escribir → escrito. Only haber changes for the person; the completed-action form stays unchanged.

example.es: Ya habíamos terminado cuando llegó Luis.
example.en: We had already finished when Luis arrived.

cards.noteEn: Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’

example.en: We have seen that movie.

cards.questionEn: How do you intensify a describing word to mean “so,” as in “so difficult”?
cards.answerEn: Put tan immediately before the word that describes the person, thing, or action.
cards.noteEn: Tan does not change form. It goes before an adjective, a word that describes a person or thing, or before an adverb, a word that describes an action. Use forms of tanto instead before a noun or when saying “so much” or “so many.”

example.en: The exam was so difficult.

cards.noteEn: Lejos describes distance. It normally appears without changing form and often follows de before the point of reference.

example.es: La estación está lejos de aquí.
example.en: The station is far from here.

cards.noteEn: Sociólogos is the masculine or mixed-group plural for people who work in sociology.

example.en: The sociologists analyzed the survey.

cards.noteEn: Psicólogos is the masculine or mixed-group plural for people who work in psychology.

example.en: Psychologists study behavior.

cards.noteEn: Biólogos is the masculine or mixed-group plural for people who work in biology.

example.en: The biologists observed the cells.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, químicos names people who work in chemistry. The same form can mean “chemical” when it describes masculine plural things.

example.en: The chemists checked the reaction.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, físicos names people who work in physics. The same written form can be an adjective meaning “physical” when it describes a plural masculine noun.

example.en: The physicists compare the data.
